h: פָּרָשַׁת זָכוֹר, מַאֲמָר ח׳ Parshas Zachor — Maamar Ches

p: זָכוֹר אֵת אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה לְךָ עֲמָלֵק וְגוֹמֵר
The mitzvah comes to remember this war;
(ח״ב בְּשַׁלַּח סה, ב; וַיַּקְהֵל קצד, ב)
"There was never a battle like this one
since the day the world was created, etc.;
וְעַל כֵּן בָּחַר מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בִּיהוֹשֻׁעַ
Therefore Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him, chose Yehoshua
to be the one who fights,
while Moshe readied himself for the battle above;
"and had Moshe not strengthened himself above
Yisrael would not have prevailed against him";
That is, besides the war below,
for the kelipah of Amalek is a barking dog,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּזּוֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (בְּשַׁלַּח סה, א)
as they said in the holy Zohar (Beshalach 65a).
And likewise Haman, of his seed —
"There is none who knows how to speak slander like Haman";
and we said that the meaning is not
that he slandered and disgraced Yisrael
רַק שֶׁיָּדַע לְקַטְרֵג עַל יִשְׂרָאֵל לְמַעְלָה
but that he knew how to prosecute against Yisrael above:
that they have slumbered from the mitzvos,
and the Rabbis — "they are one people,"
and "the laws of the King," the King of kings,
"they do not keep," and the like
(this was explained in Rosh Chodesh Adar, maamar 8,
And likewise it is stated regarding Amalek
פָּרָשָׁה יב סִימָן יג וְזֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ שָׁם)
parsha 12, siman 13, and the holy Zohar there)
that he would cut off their circumcised flesh
Meaning: even though Yisrael are circumcised,
not all of them are righteous,
for there are some who blemish
the attribute of "the tzaddik, foundation of the world."
And this is what they said in the holy Zohar
to uproot the covenant from its place, etc."
against the holiness of Yisrael's covenant and its root.
And for this Yehoshua was chosen
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּפְסִיקְתָּא (שָׁם סִימָן ה, ו)
as they said in the Pesikta (ibid., siman 5–6)
by the hand of the seed of Yosef,
for all the others he repels with claims:
The point is that Amalek is the kelipah of the dog,
which is the inner core of the ox and the donkey,
which are the kelipos of Esav and Yishmael;
and the inner letters of shor and chamor,
vav and mem-vav, equal in numerical value to kelev
(as written in the holy Zohar, Beshalach,
and the glosses of Rabbi Chaim Vital,
And Esav is the root of the kelipah of murder,
and Yishmael is the kelipah of lust, the donkey.
And Amalek, the inner core of both, prosecutes,
for in Yisrael too claims are found
with the claim of the sale of Yosef,
akin to the kelipah of jealousy and murder.
That is not so for Yosef,
against whom there is no claim at all,
for he is a chariot for the attribute of
צַדִּיק יְסוֹד עוֹלָם כַּיָּדוּעַ [זוה״ק ח״ג רלו, א]
"the tzaddik, foundation of the world," as is known (Zohar III 236a);
therefore Yehoshua, of his seed, was chosen
And Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him,
readied himself to win the battle above —
And in the holy Zohar, Vayakhel (ibid.), it is stated,
"He lay in ambush above to defile the Sanctuary,
וְכָמִין הֲוָה לְתַתָּא לְסָאֲבָא יִשְׂרָאֵל וְכוּלֵּי
and lay in ambush below to defile Yisrael, etc." —
he said, "There is set against you
to defile you on all sides,
and were it not, etc."; see there.
and this is what is called "the Sanctuary":
that is, "the heart of the wise man at his right,"
the place where Hashem Yisbarach dwells,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה ה, ב)
שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לִבָּן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל
that the Holy One, Blessed is He, is the heart of Yisrael?
For it is written (Tehillim 73:26), 'The Rock of my heart
and my portion is God forever'";
and so it is written in the holy Zohar
And it may be that what they said, "above and below,"
he cooled you off before others.
To what may this be compared?
וּבִפְסִיקְתָּא (לְפָרָשַׁת זָכוֹר פָּרָשָׁה יב סִימָן יג)
And in the Pesikta (for Parshas Zachor, parsha 12, siman 13)
the dispute mentioned is also stated,
he made you cold as water,
as in the matter of which it says (Mishlei 25:25),
וְהֵבִיא גַּם כֵּן הַמָּשָׁל עַיֵּין שָׁם
and it also brings the parable; see there.
But from the fact that it brings the verse
it appears that he gave them a sense of relief,
כְּדִמְיוֹן מַיִם קָרִים עַל נֶפֶשׁ עֲיֵפָה.
like cold water upon a weary soul.
And it appears, as we said
that Amalek is the evil inclination
that is constantly found in the body.
who lay in ambush for them, etc.,"
for he is the primordial serpent, the first serpent.
וְיוֹשֵׁב בֵּין שְׁנֵי מִפְתְּחֵי הַלֵּב וְכוּלֵּי
and sits between the two openings of the heart, etc." —
for the two chambers of the heart are
"the heart of the wise man at his right
and the heart of the fool at his left,"
as they said there regarding the kidneys,
that the good one is at his right, etc.
does not keep to its place,
and at times it misleads a person
and presents itself as standing at his right,
teaching him what will benefit him for good —
"He appeared to him as a Torah scholar,"
so that he regarded him as a rav
and did not want to walk at his right;
but Yaakov Avinu, peace be upon him,
And so with Amalek, as it is written (Devarim 25:18):
"what he did to you on the way…,
who happened upon you on the way";
[שְׁמוּאֵל-א טו, ב] אֲשֶׁר שָׂם לוֹ בַּדֶּרֶךְ וְגוֹמֵר
(I Shmuel 15:2) "how he set upon him on the way…":
"He was an evil serpent toward Yisrael,
lying in ambush for them at the crossroads."
And this is what is stated (Avos 6:4):
"This is the way of Torah, etc.,
and you shall live a life of hardship";
פִּקּוּדֵי ה׳ יְשָׁרִים מְשַׂמְּחֵי לֵב [תְּהִלִּים יט, ט]
"the precepts of Hashem are upright, gladdening the heart" (Tehillim 19:9),
that is after one merits the light of Torah;
then it brings joy into his heart.
is that he has a life of hardship —
as they said in Midrash Tanchuma
with an argument from the words of Torah,
"It is vain for you who rise early…,
who eat the bread of toil" (Tehillim 127:2) —
and this is "the bread of toil,"
which comes with sorrow and great exertion
"So He gives His beloved sleep" (Tehillim ibid.) —
וִידִידוֹ הַיְינוּ שְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
and "His beloved" is King Shlomo, peace be upon him,
entirely in sleep, in a dream,
and it is written (ibid. 24), "and Hashem loved him."
And this accords with the one who says,
אֲשֶׁר קָרְךָ עָשָׂה אוֹתְךָ קַר כַּמַּיִם
"karcha — he made you cold as water":
he came with arguments from the words of Torah
and live a life of hardship
even in the way of Torah.
And this is why they said, "as in the matter of which it says,
for he appears like one teaching him
what benefits him for his good according to the Torah.
And this is the battle above,
which is "the heart of the wise man at his right,"
the place where Hashem Yisbarach dwells.
without disguise or concealment of his face,
but standing in his own place,
in "the heart of the fool at his left,"
and to entice them into slackness
in Torah and in the mitzvos;
and this accords with the one who says,
And this is what they said,
דַּהֲוָה כָּמִין לוֹן עַל פָּרָשַׁת אָרְחִין
that he lay in ambush for them at the crossroads,
at the two openings of the heart.
And for this both Moshe and Yehoshua were needed:
for he came from the seed of Yosef,
the aspect of "the mighty one who conquers his inclination";
and Yehoshua, who brings Yisrael into the Land,
is the aspect of Torah she'b'al peh,
And Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him,
עַל דֶּרֶךְ מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה כט, א)
along the lines of what they said (Rosh Hashanah 29a):
אֶלָּא כָּל זְמַן שֶׁיִּשְׂרָאֵל מִסְתַּכְּלִין כְּלַפֵּי מַעְלָה
Rather, as long as Yisrael looked upward
to their Father in Heaven, etc."
That is, to give oneself over
and to subjugate one's heart to Him;
and then the evil inclination cannot
and clothe itself in the garb of one who guides toward good.
וְזֶה הָיָה הָרִאשׁוֹן יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
The first to do this was Yaakov Avinu, peace be upon him,
who said, "The God who has shepherded me
he gave over all his faculties to Hashem Yisbarach,
וְעַל כֵּן לֹא יָכוֹל הַס״מ לְהַטְעוֹתוֹ
therefore Samael could not mislead him.
"Yaakov is on the outside and Moshe on the inside"
as they said in Tikkunei Zohar (tikkun 13);
and he brought it about in Yisrael
that they subjugate their hearts to their Father in Heaven;
and this was Moshe's victory above:
"when he would raise his hand, Yisrael prevailed."

paragraphs.text: Zohar II 65b, Beshalach 32:18,21–22 — “‘Amalek came.’ Rabbi Shimon said: A mystery of wisdom is here. This war came from a decree of harsh judgment, and this war existed above and below. ... Moses saw and knew the root of the matter. Moses said: I will prepare myself for that war above, and you, Joshua, prepare yourself for the war below. This is what is written, ‘When Moses raised his hand, Israel prevailed’—Israel above. Therefore Moses withdrew from the war below, to exert himself in the war above, so that victory would be achieved through him.” The division of labor between Moses and Joshua is explicit, supplying the structure of Rav Tzadok’s exposition of two kinds of inward attack.

paragraphs.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Ki Teitzei 10 — “What would the house of Amalek do? They would cut off Israel’s circumcisions and throw them upward, saying: This is what You chose? Here is what You chose.” The act is presented as a deliberate taunt against the divine choice expressed by the covenant. Rav Tzadok reads its spiritual meaning as an accusation against Israel’s faithfulness.

paragraphs.text: Zohar II 194b–195a, Vayakhel 1:1–4 — “Amalek’s war was on every side, above and below, for at that time the evil serpent grew strong above and below. Just as the evil serpent lies in wait at a crossroads, so Amalek was an evil serpent toward Israel, lying in wait for them at a crossroads. ... He lay in wait above to defile the sanctuary, and lay in wait below to defile Israel. ... Had Moses not strengthened himself above and Joshua below, Israel could not have withstood him. Therefore the Holy One, blessed be He, preserves that hostility from generation to generation. Why? Because he intended to uproot the covenant from its place.” The original passage explicitly names the covenant as the object of the attack. The discussion continues across the folio boundary.

paragraphs.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Ki Teitzei 10; compare Pesikta Rabbati 12 — “Rabbi Yohanan said: All the princes of the tribes stand to contend with Esau’s prince, but he does not fall into their hands, because he answers each of them. To Reuben he says: You were suspected concerning your father’s concubine. To Shimon and Levi: You killed Shechem. To the other tribes: You sold your brother and sought to kill him. To Judah: You were suspected concerning Tamar your daughter-in-law. To Benjamin: You were suspected concerning the concubine at Gibeah. When [Joseph’s] prince comes to contend with him, he immediately falls before him, because he has no answer to give him: ‘The house of Jacob shall be fire, the house of Joseph flame, and the house of Esau straw.’” The received digital wording has “Esau’s prince” at the second encounter, although the argument and the quoted verse require Joseph’s prince. This apparent textual slip is flagged rather than hidden; the parallel Pesikta Rabbati 12 explicitly reads Joseph’s prince.

paragraphs.text: Mikdash Melekh on Zohar, II, 65a:1 — “‘Which is called a dog’: note that the middle letters of ‘ox’ and ‘donkey’—the vav of shor and the mem-vav of chamor—have the numerical value of kelev, ‘dog.’ Or Yisrael writes that they are called choshekh, ‘darkness’: chamor, shor, kelev—donkey, ox, dog.” This unsigned gloss independently verifies the letter calculation and explicitly names Or Yisrael for the acronym. It does not identify R. Chaim Vital as its author. Mikdash Melekh on Zohar I 193a quotes the same calculation in the name of the RaMaZ, R. Moshe Zacut: “Donkey, ox, dog—the dog emerges from between the ox and the donkey, whose inner letters, vav and mem-vav, equal kelev.” The Mikdash Melekh marks this as a marginal note (נ״ב) without naming its author. The Matok MiDvash page for this daf does not print the gloss, and no source located names R. Chaim Vital as its author.

paragraphs.text: Zohar III 236a, Pinchas 71:2 — “‘Moses took the bones of Joseph with him’—the bones of the Righteous One, the foundation of the worlds, the degree of Joseph the righteous. Concerning them it is said, ‘My offering, My bread for My fires.’ There is no bread except Torah: ‘Come, eat of My bread.’ They are the clusters of the Righteous One, and the Righteous One is a fruit-bearing tree.” The text directly identifies Joseph’s degree with the righteous foundation. The canonical source coordinate is preserved alongside the manuscript’s folio reference.

paragraphs.text: Pesikta Rabbati 12, exposition of “asher karekha” — “Our rabbis said: ‘He encountered you’—he made you lukewarm, he made you cold like water, as it is said, ‘Cold water upon a weary soul.’ Rabbi Huna said: To what may it be compared? To a boiling bath from which everyone fled. One person came, jumped into it, and cooled it; immediately everyone came and bathed in it. So Israel: when they came out of Egypt, all fled from them. ... Amalek came and cooled them.” The source contains both the comparison with refreshing cold water and the bath parable. Rav Tzadok distinguishes the apparent kindness of the temptation from its weakening effect.

paragraphs.text: Berakhot 61a:27–28 — “Rav said: The evil inclination resembles a fly and sits between the two openings of the heart, as it is said, ‘Dead flies make the perfumer’s oil putrid.’ ... The Sages taught: A person has two kidneys; one counsels him for good and one counsels him for evil. It is reasonable that the good one is to his right and the evil one to his left, as it is written, ‘A wise person’s heart is to his right, and a fool’s heart to his left.’” The two openings and two sides underlie Rav Tzadok’s distinction between direct enticement and evil presenting itself as good.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Bo 1 — “The evil inclination from the beginning of the kelipah does not incite openly to evil; rather he disguises himself as one guiding toward good… ‘like a Torah scholar he appeared to him.’” Rav Tzadok there traces this disguise to the serpent. “You shall surely not die” was offered as concern for Chavah’s own good, “taste only the good.” So this is the deepest root of the kelipah, which only Yaakov’s truth sees through.

paragraphs.text: Pirkei Avot 6:4 — “This is the way of Torah: Eat bread with salt, drink water by measure, sleep on the earth, live a life of hardship, and labor in Torah. If you do so, happy are you, and it is good for you: happy are you in this world, and it is good for you in the world to come.” Rav Tzadok distinguishes the difficult road of acquisition from the joy of Torah after its light is attained.

paragraphs.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Noach 3:2–3,7 — “The Oral Torah is not found with one who seeks this world’s pleasure, desire, honor, and greatness, but with one who gives his life for it. ... The Oral Torah is difficult to learn and contains great hardship; it is compared to darkness: ‘The people walking in darkness saw a great light’—these are the masters of Talmud whose eyes the Holy One illuminates in what is prohibited and permitted, impure and pure. ... It involves great hardship and lost sleep; a person wears himself out for it. Therefore its reward is in the world to come.” The Midrash gives the transition from demanding labor to illumination that the deceptive voice seeks to bypass.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Ohr HaChaim on Shemos 17:9 — “Recognizing that the sin was the neglect of the battle of Torah, Moshe said only Yehoshua is fit to go out to war, of whom it says ‘he did not depart from within the tent.’” The Ohr HaChaim gives the plain-sense reason for choosing Yehoshua that Rav Tzadok gives in Kabbalistic terms. Amalek’s claim came through Torah, so it is defeated by the one wholly bound to Torah.

paragraphs.text: Rosh Hashanah 29a:6 — “‘When Moses raised his hand, Israel prevailed.’ Do Moses’ hands make war or break war? Rather, it tells you: Whenever Israel looked upward and subjected their hearts to their Father in heaven, they grew strong; when not, they fell. ... Does the serpent kill, or does the serpent give life? Rather, whenever Israel looked upward and subjected their hearts to their Father in heaven, they were healed; when not, they wasted away.” The Mishnah places the hands of Moses and the bronze serpent under the same principle: the decisive act is directing and submitting the heart to God.
